title: Cologne Catholics once spoke like some Protestants about certain belief of personal pardon
source_text: XL. Verum est quidem Protestantes nonnullos sic loqui de illa persuasione quam fideles habent de gratia Dei & remissione peccatorum suorum, quasi in ea proprie consisteret fides justificans: sed eodem etiam modo loquuntur quidam quos Schola Romana pro Catholicis habet. Nam in libro edito a Canonicis Coloniensibus Anno 1536. in Concilio quodam Provinciali, qui liber Enchiridion Coloniense vocatur, haec expressa verba leguntur, Non jubemus ut perpetuo de justificatione & acceptatione sua dubitent homines, &c. Fatentur enim verum esse ad justificationem hominis omnino requiri ut homo certo credat, non tantum generaliter quod propter Christum vere poenitentibus remittantur peccata, sed quod ipsimet homini credenti remissa sunt propter Christum per fidem, &c. Quibus consentit liber qui dicitur Antididagma, & cujus authores sunt iidem Colonienses. Dicunt enim authorem illi, titulo de Justificatione, Nos justificari per fidem, qua absque dubitatione firmiter confidimus nobis qui veram poenitentiam habemus, peccata nostra propter Christum esse remissa. Ac quemadmodum Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae aliud jam hac de re sentiunt, sic rem eandem aliter explicant plerique saltem Theologi Ecclesiae Reformatae, nec inter actus fidei ad justificationem coram Deo praevios ponunt, ut diximus, persuasionem de facta jam nostri cum Deo reconciliatione, sed solum fiduciam de illa obtinenda.
pass_a_gloss: It is true indeed that some Protestants so speak of that persuasion which the faithful have concerning God’s grace and the remission of their sins, as if justifying faith properly consisted in it: but in the same way also speak certain ones whom the Roman School holds for Catholics. For in a book published by the Canons of Cologne in the year 1536 in a certain Provincial Council, which book is called the Cologne Enchiridion, these express words are read: We do not command that people perpetually doubt concerning their justification and acceptance, &c. For they confess it to be true that for a person’s justification it is altogether required that the person certainly believe, not only generally that for Christ’s sake sins are remitted to the truly penitent, but that to this very believing person sins have been remitted for Christ’s sake through faith, &c. With which agrees the book called Antididagma, whose authors are the same Colonienses. For those authors say, under the title On Justification, that we are justified by faith by which without doubt we firmly trust that for us who have true repentance our sins have been remitted for Christ’s sake. And just as the doctors of the Roman Church now think otherwise on this matter, so at least most theologians of the Reformed Church explain the same matter otherwise, and among the acts of faith prior to justification before God they do not place, as we have said, persuasion concerning our reconciliation with God already made, but only trust concerning obtaining it.
pass_b_english: Even sixteenth-century Cologne Catholics once urged certain personal belief of pardon.
Le Blanc notes both Rome and many Reformed now refuse to make already-granted reconciliation the prior act of justifying faith.
